graduation_requirements.raw_text: A total of 96 credits and 40 hours of community service are required to graduate, students are also required to document appropriate progress towards meeting the BUHS transferable skills. Students are required to meet proficiency indicators in each BUHS course and score a grade of 60% or higher to receive course credit. The distribution requirements are given below: Required Credits English* 16 Social Studies* 12 Mathematics* 12 Science* 12 Physical Education 6** Health Education 2 Fine Arts 4 Electives 32 Total credits 96 *Career Center courses may serve as equivalents to fulfill some of these required high school courses. *Students must take English in 9th, 10th and 11th grade. ** Beginning for the Class of 2030 the number of required PE credits to graduate goes from 4 to 6. Virtual High School (VHS), Independent Study (IS) (approved well in advance), and certain athletic participation may serve as alternatives to some courses. VHS may only be used to fulfill elective credit. COMMUNITY SERVICE BUHS believes that community service is a worthwhile and rewarding experience for all high school students. It strengthens our community and contributes to personal growth. Through community service a BUHS student can demonstrate proficiency in the transferable skill “Responsible and Involved citizenship”. We have, therefore, a graduation requirement of 40 HOURS of community service. You can volunteer for a non-profit organization or a worthy individual who is not related to you or a member of your household. A non-profit organization is not a business but is an agency which serves the needs of a group of people or the community. Any other community service proposals should be approved in advance by a BUHS administrator. Service hours must be documented on the BUHS Community Service Form. A student may begin accumulating hours to meet this requirement during the summer immediately preceding 9th grade. For students who transfer to BUHS after 9th grade, the requirement is prorated to five hours per semester.

This course is being specifically designed to offer more English electives to 9th and 10th graders. There will be substantial choice reading in the class as well as revisiting classics in the Graphic Novel format. This class will also explore creativity and technology as students develop their own Graphic novels, with or without the help of tech programs. courses.description: When we think of the magic of theatre, we often think about the performances of the actors, the lights, the costumes, or the sets–but none of those things are possible without the work of the playwright. In this course, we will explore the process that goes into writing a play. We’ll begin by examining what a playwright actually does, while exploring and addressing preconceived notions students may have regarding playwriting. We’ll consider where playwrights find their ideas, and how they employ character and conflict to create a piece of theatre. As part of the learning process, students will write and workshop monologues and short plays with their colleagues, learning how to give and receive peer-to-peer feedback. And, as plays are meant to be staged, not read, students will also perform their work in class, both on their own and with their colleagues. This course assumes grade-level reading, writing, speaking, and problem-solving skills. MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any other English course.

The class is challenging and will take greater time and effort than other electives. Students who choose it should have strong English skills and thorough preparation for literary studies. The study of journalism is an effective way to develop both reading and writing skills, the foundations of literacy. The two underlying beliefs of this intensive journalistic writing course are as follows: (1) a command of clear, concise language leads to effective written and spoken communication; and (2) students who take an intensive journalistic writing course learn skills useful in any field of endeavor. Through writing, reading, viewing, and discussing, students in this course will learn the principles of ethical journalism, interviewing techniques, news writing, editing, and newspaper design. In addition, students will read and discuss the work of professional journalists. Class members will contribute to the student newspaper, THE BRATTLEBORO BEACON. This course is a prerequisite for Advanced Journalism. MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options.

There will be a variety of texts and media, including novels and long-form non-fiction. There will be regular reading homework and regular writing assignments. Readings may include such titles as Hamlet, Brave New World, Cat’s Cradle, Feed, and Between the World and Me, as well as a variety of short fiction, articles, poetry, and film. courses.description: Restorative Justice—or, transformative justice, restorative practices, transformative practices, etc.—is a concept as old as the human community itself. Often contrasted against contemporary criminal justice, with its emphasis on punishment and isolation, restorative justice seeks to address harm, provide restitution and vindication to those harmed, and, when possible, reintegrate the offender into the community through personal transformation. In short: we all live and work together, and we need each other, and when conflict and offense arises, we seek to heal rather than ignore, condemn, segregate, or punish. In this elective, we will study the origins and practice of restorative justices throughout history and in contemporary society. We will engage in personal and transpersonal practices aimed at re-imagining our roles and relationships as members of the community. Students will examine individual historical situations where restorative justice was or could have been employed, and students will develop transformative justice plans based on real and imagined circumstances. Finally, students will focus on one or several aspects of the approach and historical context as the basis of a research paper and presentation. Students in this class will be invited to engage more deeply with BUHS’s evolving Restorative Justice program, whether participating in circles, developing protocols, or working on peer outreach. Texts may include: The Little Book of Race and Restorative Justice, by Fania E. Davis; selections from Restoring Justice: an Introduction, by Daniel W. Van Ness; selections from The Big Book of Restorative Justice, edited by Howard Zehr. MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options.

As we read some classic children’s books, we’ll also be reading about the philosophy, psychology, sociology, history, and cultural connections of the books, in addition to literary criticism and film adaptations. This course is designed to mimic a discussion-based college seminar class and is fast-paced. Expect to do annotations, light research, bi-weekly essays, and daily discussions. We will dive deeply into the literature we read and will cover quite a bit of ground during the course. This will be a scholarly look at what seems to be a very simple subject. *This course may be taken for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT. courses.description: Television Production is designed to encourage students to develop the necessary skills to write, film, and perform all aspects of a television broadcast. In addition, students will learn to program the various technical equipment, film effectively, create special effects, and newscasts, work with Adobe Photoshop to create graphics, edit films using iMovie and FinalCut Pro, and air their broadcasts to the greater Brattleboro community. The students will be responsible for creating and airing a live broadcast at least three times a week. In addition to the broadcasts, students will compose short films, commercials, and documentaries and will also be expected to film school events such as sports games. Students in this class must be motivated and self-directed with the ability to adapt to unexpected change. They must also be able to work closely as part of a team. Solid communication skills (public speaking, reading, and writing), and strong computer skills are strongly recommended. MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options.

courses.description: In this upperclassman elective, students will engage in research and produce comprehensive papers in three major academic formats: MLA (Modern Language Association), APA (American Psychological Association), and CMS (Chicago Manual of Style). The instructor places emphasis on research methods, organization and construction, and revision. Much of this class is student-driven—half of each week will be spent working independently on research (reading, researching, note-taking, or composing); while the instructor is available to advise, assist, and direct, completion of this course is contingent on students’ ability to manage time, material, and long-term plans. Students will need to undertake a substantial amount of reading and composition outside class in order to achieve our goals. MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of English 1 or English 1 Advanced and a second course in English.

courses.description: This course requires students to submit a completed course contract and to complete substantial pre-course assignments. Students who complete this course are also required to take the corresponding Advanced Placement English Language and Composition exam in May. This course was designed according to guidelines set by the Advanced Placement Program of the College Board. This course engages students in becoming skilled readers of prose written in a variety of periods, disciplines, and contexts. Students become skilled writers who compose for a variety of purposes and in a variety of forms: narrative, exploratory, expository, argumentative, and on a variety of subjects from personal experiences to public policy, from imaginative literature to popular culture. The overarching purpose is to enable students to read complex texts with understanding and to write prose of sufficient richness and complexity to communicate with mature readers. Readings may include: Friday Night Lights, Narrative of Frederick Douglass, I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings, 1984, Nickel and Dimed and Into the Wild, in addition to articles, short stories, poems, and speeches for stylistic analysis. MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion English 1 or English 1 Advanced and a second course in English

courses.description: Students in this course will read, analyze, and create literature in three different genres: poetry, short fiction, and personal essay. There is an emphasis on vocabulary, peer editing, and revision. Students who enroll should be prepared to read and write responses to peer work weekly, to work in small workshop groups, and to engage in bold experimentation with their own craft; as such, this is a course for brave students who love literature, art, and discussion. Alternates with Intro to Poetry MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of English 1 or English 1 Advanced and second course in English

courses.description: This semester-long elective course will utilize sports as a lens to look deeply into human nature and culture. Examining texts about competition, spectacle, personal struggle, and personal triumph, we will consider the positive themes of heroism, pride, leadership, and identity and the negative themes of disappointment, corruption, scandal, racism, sexism, and misuse of power. Literature may be chosen from among the following texts: The Boys in the Boat, Born to Run, Shoeless Joe, Little Girls in Pretty Boxes, Friday Night Lights, The Crossover, Furia, In These Girls Hope is a Muscle, Gym Candy, as well as poems, short stories, current articles, and films. (THIS COURSE ALTERNATES WITH ADVENTURE READING) MAY NOT be taken concurrently with any first or second course options.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of English 1 or English 1 Advanced and a second course in English.

courses.description: Students enrolled in this course receive instruction in language and academic learning strategies for student success. The course supports development of academic language skills (listening, reading, speaking and writing) in the areas of mathematics, science, social studies, ELA and general instruction. Students analyze similarities in language expectations across these content areas, and develop proficiency across them. An emphasis on post-secondary planning and career options is interwoven into this applied-learning class.
courses.notes: Credit value taken from department introduction (p.34): "ELL Content Support (2 credits)"

courses.description: This course highlights skills, and language needed to add English as a New Language. Using the theme of Community, students work on beginning English skills, introduction to literacy, and phonemic awareness. A strong emphasis is placed on orientation to school systems and communities for social-cultural adjustment.
courses.notes: ELL course for the WIDA proficiency level named in the title

courses.description: This course builds on foundational knowledge in Entering English to increase communicative competence beyond basic English proficiency into a wider array of language tasks and skills. Students at this level have mastered the state standards for Entering level. Students at Emerging Level build vocabulary and literacy skills, using a reading series based on progressively difficult text. They begin to work with formal grammar points, precise vocabulary, and idioms. Students learn to format paragraphs, letters, and short oral presentations after cooperative group projects.
courses.notes: ELL course for the WIDA proficiency level named in the title

courses.description: Building on foundational skills in the first two English Proficiency Levels, the Developing course, increases the diversity of language skills, technical vocabulary, and uses of language across a wide range of topics and content areas. A priority is placed on building academic literacy in English, relying on students’ strengths in other proficiency areas. Students are introduced to a wide variety of communication genres including informational text, expository writing, poetry, narratives, and autobiographies.
courses.notes: ELL course for the WIDA proficiency level named in the title

courses.description: This class focuses on refining language and expression through advanced English language experiences across a wide range of content areas for English development. Advanced grammar and vocabulary study are woven into the curriculum, which often focuses on exploring post-secondary options and planning for the future. Increased independent and project-based learning, allow for individualized study and language development according to student goals. Reading and writing of extensive expository and fictional text are part of the language experience.
courses.notes: ELL course for the WIDA proficiency level named in the title

courses.description: This class prepares students to meet exit criteria from the ELL program. It works with advanced language topics and projects to develop full proficiency in English. Projects may include advanced vocabulary and grammar study, and analysis of fiction and nonfiction texts. Research reports and English projects for a wide variety of purposes continue to support the language acquisition process to ideally support students' multilingualism to the maximum benefit to the learner.
courses.notes: ELL course for the WIDA proficiency level named in the title

courses.description: This course emphasizes the conceptual skills of Algebra. Special attention is given to the abstract developmental structure of mathematics and to the student acquiring problem solving skills to be both applied and used as a learning strategy.
courses.prerequisites: Recommendation of Current Teacher
courses.notes: Catalog level: Level 1 accelerated sequence (p.35)

courses.description: This course consists of a Euclidean approach to plane and solid geometry. Emphasis is placed on deductive reasoning and formal proof using postulates, definitions, and theorems. Methods of inductive reasoning are explored through the use of dynamic geometry software.
courses.prerequisites: 80 or better in Accelerated Algebra 1 or recommendation of Algebra 1 teacher
courses.notes: Catalog level: Level 1 accelerated sequence (p.35)

courses.description: This course is a continuation of Accelerated Algebra One. Topics include graphing systems of linear equations and a graphical analysis of higher order polynomials. The student studies manipulation of algebraic expressions, particularly those containing rational exponents and radicals. *This course may also be offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT.
courses.prerequisites: 80 or better in Accelerated Algebra 1
courses.notes: Catalog level: Level 1 accelerated sequence (p.35). Catalog notes this course may also be offered for college credit (see DUAL ENROLLMENT)

courses.description: This course prepares students for, and is the principal prerequisite for, AP calculus. The student studies elementary functions including: transformations, combinations of functions, inverse functions, polynomial, exponential, logarithmic, rational and trigonometric functions with an emphasis on their unifying properties. Sinusoidal functions and oblique triangle trigonometry are studied in depth. Literal derivation of basic formulas, individual and group projects, and problem solving are key components of this course. It is assumed that a student taking this course is self- motivated and genuinely interested in an exploratory approach to learning mathematics. The level of success students will experience in this course is directly related to how well they have internalized the skills and concepts studied in their previous mathematics courses.
courses.prerequisites: 80 or better in Accelerated Algebra 2 and Accelerated Geometry
courses.notes: Catalog level: Level 1 accelerated sequence (p.35)

courses.description: Statistics is an introduction to the basic ideas and techniques of probability and statistics. Topics included are: numerical and graphical descriptive measures, probability, random variables, probability distributions (binomial, geometric and the normal), sampling theory, estimation and confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, use of the correlation coefficient in making predictions from regression equations (both linear and nonlinear). Numerical calculations of the above will be done using technology. *This course may also be offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT.
courses.prerequisites: 75 or better in Algebra 2
courses.notes: Catalog notes this course may also be offered for college credit (see DUAL ENROLLMENT)

courses.description: A college level course in differential and integral calculus which was designed according to guidelines set by the Advanced Placement Program of the College Board. Prepares the student for the Calculus AB Advanced Placement Examination.
courses.prerequisites: 80 or better in Accelerated Pre-Calculus

courses.description: A standard beginning Algebra course consisting of properties of real numbers; solving linear equations and inequalities; graphing linear functions; writing linear equations to solve word problems; solving systems of linear equations, exponential functions and data and statistics.
courses.prerequisites: Teacher recommendation

courses.description: This course offers a Euclidean approach to plane geometry which includes a study of the properties of polygons, (especially triangles and quadrilaterals), parallelism, perpendicularity, and circles. The student also studies the concepts and applications of congruence, similarity, and coordinate geometry.
courses.prerequisites: 75% or better in Algebra 1

courses.description: This course is a continuation of Algebra One. The student studies the applications of the real number system to solving second degree equations, factoring polynomials and solving exponential functions using logarithms. Topics include graphing with an emphasis on solving systems of equations and quadratics. Students interested in taking this course who do not meet the prerequisite criteria above should consult with their previous math teacher and counselor.
courses.prerequisites: 75% or better in Algebra 1

courses.description: In this course the student will be exposed to functions including, polynomial, exponential, logarithmic, rational, and trigonometric. Students will study the parent function and shifts that can be applied to the parent function as well as the inverses of these functions and their applications in real world situations. Personal ownership of a scientific calculator is highly recommended for students taking this course. Students interested in taking this course who do not meet the prerequisite criteria above should consult with their previous math teacher and counselor.
courses.prerequisites: 75% or better in Algebra 1 and Geometry

courses.description: This is an introductory course intended to prepare students for Algebra. Emphasis is placed on covering the most fundamental standard in the Common Core State Standards in mathematics. The pace of the course is adjusted so that careful attention can be given to reinforcing skills necessary for success in future math courses. Content standards will focus on: Ratios and Proportional Relationships, The Number System, Expressions And Equations, Functions, Geometry, Statistics and Probability.
courses.prerequisites: Teacher recommendation

courses.description: This course is designed to help students develop the knowledge and skills necessary to make sound personal financial decisions. Exploring the importance of a budget, learning to maintain a savings plan, realizing the importance of investing and planning for retirement, and managing risk. Students will recognize the importance of taking responsibility for their own financial well-being and examine how their daily decisions around money affect their future financial success.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra 1 and any Geometry

courses.course_name: Intro to Coding and Computer Science
courses.description: Students taking Introduction to Coding and Computer Science will learn the foundations of computer science and coding using the Javascript language. The course allows students to build understanding of variables, data types, logical operators, conditional statements, loops, arrays, and functions, using an engaging, highly graphical coding environment.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra 1 and Geometry with a grade of 75 or above or with department head approval.

courses.description: The student will acquire the basic skills of mathematics through the discovery and application of problem solving strategies. The student will also acquire the ability to communicate mathematically, both orally and in writing and should expect to work collaboratively with fellow students in small groups, and to make class presentations. Topics may include: probability, tessellation and other geometric concepts, logical reasoning, drawings and diagrams, coordinate geometry, and algebra. There will be high expectations for in-class participation and productivity.
courses.prerequisites: Algebra 1 and Geometry

courses.description: An independent project of the student’s choosing. This offering is not intended to duplicate existing courses and is not eligible for core credit. Content should be determined in consultation with the Mathematics Department as early as possible. The student must find a faculty mentor to monitor this study
courses.prerequisites: With the approval of the head of the mathematics department

courses.description: The required first course in the BUHS Science sequence provides students with a study of Earth and its place in the universe. Topics may include: the history of Earth, plate tectonics, weathering, erosion and deposition, climate, space systems and human sustainability. The common thread is how everything changes over time. We will connect what we learn to issues of human impact, climate change and sustainability. How are we humans changing our planet?
courses.fulfills_text: The required first course in the BUHS Science sequence

courses.description: Students are introduced to fundamental concepts of biology including biochemistry, the living cell, characteristics of life, evolution and genetics. A variety of lab exercises and problem solving activities will be used to demonstrate these principles. A term project, the Capstone, presented by the student to the class, may be a culmination of student research and understanding
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of ESS
courses.fulfills_text: 2nd Required

courses.description: This course is designed to provide students with a background in physical science in a lab-based setting. Students will gain an understanding of the fundamental concepts of matter and its interactions. Topics may include energy, waves, and electricity and magnetism. Students who complete Introduction to Chemistry and Physics may continue on to take all 4th and beyond science courses. Students wanting to take AP Physics after taking the Fundamentals of Chemistry and Physics, should first take either a full semester of Chemistry or Physics.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of ESS and Biology
courses.fulfills_text: 3rd Required (Introduction to Chemistry and Physics, or Chemistry or Physics)

courses.description: Physics is a college preparatory course that will probe the fundamental laws of nature which serve as a foundation of all natural phenomena. This course will offer a traditional, mathematically and conceptually based study of classical mechanics, force, motion, energy, thermodynamics, wave motion and light or electricity and magnetism. Historical background of natural philosophy as related to physics will also be included. Students are expected to solve problems, do laboratory work, maintain an organized science notebook , and display effective work and study habits.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of ESS and Biology; completed Algebra 2 with 80% or higher or recommendation of Algebra & Biology teachers
courses.fulfills_text: 3rd Required (Introduction to Chemistry and Physics, or Chemistry or Physics)

courses.description: Chemistry is a math-based physical science course designed for students planning to attend college with the possibility of majoring in a science. The course requires excellent study skills, time management, and the use of a scientific calculator in solving problems. Students entering Chemistry are expected to use algebra with minimal review. Chemistry has a strong laboratory component. Students may be required to develop and maintain a science laboratory notebook. Portions of the lab program support student participation in lab design using logical problem solving skills. Topics may include: a review of matter and scientific measurement, quantum mechanics and the periodic table, chemical bonding and chemical reactions, the mole and stoichiometry, the behavior of gasses, solutions chemistry, acid-base chemistry, oxidation-reduction reactions, and thermochemistry. A term project will be required of all Chemistry students.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Algebra 1, ESS and Biology with 80% or higher
courses.fulfills_text: 3rd Required (Introduction to Chemistry and Physics, or Chemistry or Physics)

courses.description: The full-year AP Physics sequence would be an excellent background for students interested in pursuing science, engineering, medical, or related majors in college. The purpose of this course is for students to learn college level physics content with high school support as well as to prepare for success to prepare for the College Board’s AP Physics exam. AP Physics topics will include kinematics, dynamics, work and energy, and gravitation, rotation and fluids. Demonstrated ability in algebra techniques is required. Students will be expected to work at a high academic level at a rapid pace in problem solving, laboratory investigations, and independently directed project work. Students are required to take the AP Physics 1 exam in the spring and complete a design project following the exam.
courses.prerequisites: Application process through Science Department; Pre-Calculus, and 3 science courses (Students who have completed Accelerated Algebra II with an 85% may take AP Physics while taking Pre-Calc.)
courses.fulfills_text: NOTE: While electives within the science department may sometimes be taken out of sequence they do NOT serve as Science graduation requirements with the exception of AP Physics.

courses.description: Wildlife Ecology and Management is a course about the ecology and wildlife of New England. Areas of Study include population dynamics, forest management, aquatic ecology, fisheries management, wildlife management and the natural history of species found in New England. Students enrolled in this course will be expected to participate in field work on a regular basis. Students will be expected to work independently and cooperatively on field studies and projects.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of ESS and Biology
courses.fulfills_text: This course is an elective and will not count toward BUHS Science Graduation Requirements.

courses.description: This elective course provides students with a neuroscience-based introduction to core themes in psychology, including sensation and perception, the neuroscience of memory, emotions, and behavior, and the diagnosis and treatment of psychological disorders. Students will need to work effectively both independently and in groups. Lab activities will be an important part of our learning. A term project may be a culmination of student research and understanding.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of ESS and Biology
courses.fulfills_text: This course is an elective and will not count toward BUHS Science Graduation Requirements.

courses.description: This course is a Science Department offering open to all grade levels with a particular focus on ninth and tenth grade students who may wish to continue their studies in Environmental Science at BUHS. Students will use the Next Generation Science and Engineering Practices to study real world problems, engaging critical thinking skills to analyze these challenges and formulate solutions. Topic areas will include: how climate has influenced human settlement over time and how humans are now impacting Earth systems; natural resource management and sustainability; forecasting the impacts of climate change; and how we can reduce the effects of human impact through mitigation and adaptation.
courses.fulfills_text: This course is an elective course and does not count toward BUHS Science Graduation Requirements.

courses.description: This course is a Science Department offering to students of all grade levels with the caveat that only students proficient in Algebra 1 and Geometry will have the necessary skills for this course. This course will offer a mathematical and conceptual understanding of orbital dynamics, stellar fusion, and cosmology along with an overview of solar system environments. An historical background of the discovery and exploration of space will also be included. Students are expected to solve problems, complete laboratory work, use computational thinking, and create an engineering design project. Through the comparison of different planetary environments, we will investigate the climate crisis on Earth. This course will provide cross-disciplinary earth science, physical science, life science, and science and engineering practices.
courses.prerequisites: Passed Algebra I and Geometry with an 85 or better, or by permission of a math teacher; Successful completion of ESS.
courses.fulfills_text: This course is an elective and will not count toward BUHS Science Graduation Requirements.

courses.description: Chemistry, or Physics is preferred but students may take these concurrently with your Biology teacher’s recommendation. This course is an elective and will not count toward BUHS Science Graduation Requirements. Advanced Biology is a course for college-bound seniors who have excelled in Biology and previous science course work and are motivated to pursue detailed study in the biological sciences. The focus of this course is the human body and will serve as an excellent preparation for later studies in anatomy and physiology. Human Impact will be studied as relates to human health and disease. The complementarity of structure and function (anatomy and physiology) is a central component of the course which includes opportunities for several dissections. A significant portion of time will be devoted to laboratory activities, problem solving, and group discussion and student presentations. A significant amount of work will be expected outside of class in order to be prepared for laboratory work and seminar discussions within the class
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Earth and Space Science, and Biology. Successful completion of IPC,
courses.offering_note: Schedule as printed: Semester: (Every other year, 26-27 next offering)

courses.prerequisites: Three Science courses and extensive interest and initiative. Arrangements must be made with a science instructor with permission of the head of the science department.
courses.fulfills_text: This course is an elective and will not count toward BUHS Science Graduation Requirements.

courses.description: Environmental Science and Policy is an intensive, interdisciplinary course that emphasizes ecosystems, resource use, human population, energy use, climate and agriculture. We study the policies and history that drive how these topics play out in America and worldwide. Students in ES&P work hard to discern the truth in these ever-controversial topics, looking at data, its interpretation and its sources. Environmental Science and Policy is a reading and writing intensive course that draws exclusively from college level material. A willingness and commitment to working hard is necessary for success in this rigorous course. *This course may also be offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT.
courses.prerequisites: Honors level work in ESS, Biology, Introduction to Chemistry and Physics, or either Chemistry or Physics and teacher recommendation.
courses.fulfills_text: This course is an elective and will not count toward BUHS Science Graduation Requirements.
courses.offering_note: Schedule as printed: Semester: (Every other year, offered 27-28); Not running in 2026-27
courses.notes: Catalog notes this course may also be offered for college credit (see DUAL ENROLLMENT)

courses.description: An examination of the culture, geography, and history in world culture regions aligned with the Common Core State Standards. While learning about our changing world, the student will be better informed about the dynamics of the earth/human situation, will strengthen existing Social Studies skills, and will begin to develop a global perspective on the present and the future. Students can expect a variety of learning activities in the course which will include discussions, lectures, written assignments, audio-visual experiences, map work, simulation/games, debates, and personal contact with people of other cultures. World Cultures and Geography meets a social studies school requirement for graduation.
courses.fulfills_text: World Cultures and Geography meets a social studies school requirement for graduation.

courses.description: In this political science course students will examine global political structures, institutions and systems. Using the comparative method, students will compare and contrast the political structures of several different states. They will develop the skills to compare and contrast the nature of these states and will use current political events to enhance their understanding. Some of the themes and concepts under study will include: political ideologies, systems of government, international relations, international political organizations, development and underdevelopment, civil society, power, sovereignty, citizenship, economic systems and public policy. Comparative Politics and Current Events meets a social studies school requirement for graduation.
courses.fulfills_text: Comparative Politics and Current Events meets a social studies school requirement for graduation.

courses.description: This is an interdisciplinary course that helps students to identify and respond to issues of bias and discrimination in society. It combines history and civics content. Students will learn about the social, political, and economic structures in society, including why they were designed and who they benefit. Students will also learn about different ways that individuals and groups have created change within society. The course is designed to help students become active and engaged participants in society. Diversity, Equity, and Civic Action meets a social studies school requirement for graduation.
courses.prerequisites: World Cultures and Geography or Comparative Politics
courses.fulfills_text: Diversity, Equity, and Civic Action meets a social studies school requirement for graduation.

courses.course_name: United States in the World 1 1870 to 1945
courses.description: A survey of the social, political and economic history of Vermont, the United States, and the World from 1870 through 1945 aligned with the Common Core State Standards. Teachers will strive to relate historical events in perspective to contemporary issues. Emphasis is placed on writing, study skills and critical thinking as well as the development of concepts related to history and social studies. A wide variety of teaching materials and methods are applied throughout the course. Students will be asked to conduct personal research as well as maintain knowledge of contemporary events. US in the World 1: 1870 to 1945 meets a social studies school requirement for graduation.
courses.prerequisites: One of the 9th grade options and Diversity, Equity, and Civic Action
courses.fulfills_text: US in the World 1: 1870 to 1945 meets a social studies school requirement for graduation.

courses.course_name: United States in the World 2 1945 to Present
courses.description: A survey of the social, political and economic history of Vermont, the United States, and the World from 1945 to the present, aligned with the Common Core State Standards. Teachers will strive to relate historical events in perspective to contemporary issues. Emphasis is placed on writing, study skills and critical thinking as well as the development of concepts related to history and social studies. A wide variety of teaching materials and methods are applied throughout the course. Students will be asked to conduct personal research as well as maintain knowledge of contemporary events. US in the World 2: 1945 to the Present meets a social studies school requirement for graduation.
courses.prerequisites: One of the 9th grade options and Diversity, Equity, and Civic Action
courses.fulfills_text: US in the World 2: 1945 to the Present meets a social studies school requirement for graduation.

courses.course_name: Social Studies Seminar: Black American History
courses.description: This course is a comprehensive exploration of the rich and complex history of Black Americans. It delves into the multifaceted experiences of Black people in the United States, from the era of enslavement to the 20th century. By examining the economic, social, political, and cultural contributions of Black Americans, students will gain a deeper understanding of their impact on American history. By the end of this course, students will have a nuanced understanding of the historical experiences of Black Americans and their enduring contributions to American society.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of three required social studies courses

courses.description: The AP U.S. History course focuses on developing students’ understanding of American history from approximately 1491 to the present. The course has students investigate the content of U.S. history for significant events, individuals, developments, and processes in nine historical periods, and develop and use the same thinking skills and methods (analyzing primary and secondary sources, making historical comparisons, chronological reasoning, and argumentation) employed by historians when they study the past. The course also provides seven themes (American and national identity; migration and settlement; politics and power; work, exchange, and technology; America in the world; geography and the environment; and culture and society) that students explore throughout the course in order to make connections among historical developments in different times and places. College Course Equivalent AP U.S. History is designed to be the equivalent of a two-semester introductory college or university U.S. history course. Students electing this course will be required to take the AP U.S. History exam. AP US History meets a social studies school requirement for graduation. Advanced Placement United States History will count as meeting 8 credit requirements.
courses.prerequisites: Completion of English 1 and 2 and Completion of Diversity, Equity, and Civic Action
courses.fulfills_text: AP US History meets a social studies school requirement for graduation. Advanced Placement United States History will count as meeting 8 credit requirements.
courses.offering_note: Schedule as printed: Full Year / Block
courses.notes: Summer reading required

courses.description: The course provides an introductory study of sociology using the principles and methods of social sciences and the scientific method. Sociological principles, sociological perspectives, and the relationship of the individual to societal groups will be emphasized. Culture and the elements influencing society today are major themes of the course. Other topics that will be examined include socialization, social structure, stratification, race, class, family, education, population, economics, religion, gender, age, and social change. Sociological research and the role of sociologists in the modern world are discussed. Students learn to think critically about the nature of society and social institutions. Large and small group discussion is emphasized. A number of papers will also be required
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of three required social studies courses

courses.description: The course provides an introductory study of sociology using the principles and methods of social sciences and the scientific method. Sociological principles, sociological perspectives, and the relationship of the individual to societal groups will be emphasized. Culture and the elements influencing society today are major themes of the course. Other topics that will be examined include socialization, social structure, stratification, race, class, family, education, population, economics, religion, gender, age, and social change. Sociological research and the role of sociologists in the modern world are discussed. Students learn to think critically about the nature of society and social institutions. Large and small group discussion is emphasized. A number of papers will also be required. A college level textbook will be utilized in this course. *This course is offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of three required social studies courses
courses.notes: Dual enrollment (college credit) course per catalog; see DUAL ENROLLMENT, pp.15-18

courses.description: This dual-credit course is an overview of constitutional, criminal, and civil law. The course emphasizes active citizenship and the balance between individual liberties and security. Learning will be facilitated through discussion, group work, simulations, case studies, research, presentations, guest speakers, and independent projects. All students will have the option of engaging in an internship or project out in the community. In addition, the class will take part in field studies at the District Court of Vermont and at the Southern Vermont Correctional Facility. The class makes use of a wide variety of materials, including various texts, readings, videos, periodicals, and internet resources. *This course is offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of three required social studies courses
courses.notes: Dual enrollment (college credit) course per catalog; see DUAL ENROLLMENT, pp.15-18

courses.description: The ability to mentor is a valued competency in business, non-profit, academic, civic and team environments. This course is intended to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of concepts, principles and practice of mentoring through theoretical and practical applications. Students will develop the necessary knowledge and skills needed to foster or create and maintain effective mentoring relationships. Topics include: creating mentoring relationships, stages of mentoring, understanding learning styles; working with groups vs. individuals and managing difficult conversations. A major component of this course will be field work in which students will be expected to select a mentoring project. Examples include: developing programs for students transitioning into BUHS, middle school leadership teams and Big Brothers/Big Sisters. *This course is offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of three required social studies courses
courses.notes: Dual enrollment (college credit) course per catalog; see DUAL ENROLLMENT, pp.15-18

courses.description: This course provides a foundation in the basic concepts upon which our economic system operates. Students study current economic issues and problems as they relate to producers, consumers, government, labor, management, and finance. Extensive reading, research, and writing are course expectations. Special emphasis is given to the examination and development of economic case studies resulting in students-designed case studies. In addition, class activities include seminars, group work, lectures, simulations, and presentations by guest speakers and student use of the Internet to obtain current data and research materials. Assessment of progress is based on the analysis of class participation, research, homework, quizzes, and tests. *This course is offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of three required social studies courses
courses.notes: Dual enrollment (college credit) course per catalog; see DUAL ENROLLMENT, pp.15-18

courses.course_name: U.s. History Through Film and Music
courses.description: The US History Through Film and Music course will offer students a different way to explore themes of US history through the lens of film and music. Students will learn how to critically analyze film and music, while gaining new insight into historical events of the 18th, 19th and 20th Centuries. This class will require students to work collaboratively both in discussion groups and on projects, as well as to complete independent writing.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of three required social studies courses

courses.description: This course focuses on the election process and the way in which local, state, and national government is organized. A key element of this course is the requirement that students become active participants in the events and activities of an election campaign or by direct involvement in government services. Special features of this class include presentations by candidates, elected and appointed government officials, and the media. Students are accountable for completion of reading, research and writing activities both in and out of class. When feasible, field studies are conducted to provide exposure to the activities of government. Assessment of progress is based on the analysis of completed assignments, class participation, research, quizzes and tests . *This course is offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of three required social studies courses
courses.notes: Dual enrollment (college credit) course per catalog; see DUAL ENROLLMENT, pp.15-18

courses.description: This two-credit course examines the American Revolution and the Civil War, with a particular focus on the political and philosophical developments that led to the Revolution, key military turning points, debates over government and representation, and the Revolution's impact from the late 18th century to the present. The course concludes by exploring how unresolved conflicts over slavery and citizenship during the Revolutionary period led to the outbreak of the American Civil War. Students will be empowered to think critically about questions of power, government, human rights, representation, and how historical events continue to shape the country today.

The 20th Century has been called a century of genocide. Why? This course will explore five genocides that occurred in the last century. Beginning with a half semester spent on the study of the Holocaust students will use personal testimonies, literature, research, and video to gather a full understanding of the causes and effects of the Holocaust. The second half of the semester will be spent exploring and comparing the cause and effects of genocides in the Ottoman Empire, Cambodia, Bosnia, and Rwanda. Much of the class depends on student discussion, participation, reading, writing and research. There will be opportunities to attend events outside of BUHS. * This course may also be offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of three required social studies courses
courses.notes: Catalog notes this course may also be offered for college credit (see DUAL ENROLLMENT)

courses.description: Students in Latin I are introduced to basic Latin vocabulary and grammar through direct readings in Latin, using the textbook Lingua Latina Per Se Illustrata. These readings focus on the daily life of a typical upper-class Roman family in the second century A.D. Latin I students begin to make linguistic connections to English and other modern languages. In addition to studying the language itself, students also begin to learn about Roman history and culture. Themes: Themes explored in Latin 1 include the provinces of the Roman Empire, daily life, family roles, slavery, the structure of a Roman house, travel in the Ancient World, and Roman mythology.

Students in Latin II develop and expand their Latin skills through direct readings in Latin, using the textbook Lingua Latina Per Se Illustrata. Latin II students continue to make linguistic connections to English and other modern languages. In addition to studying the language itself, students also continue to learn about Roman history and culture. Themes: Themes explored in Latin II include animals, medicine, the military, the Roman calendar, education, sea travel, and advanced numbers and letters.

Students in Latin III continue to develop and expand their Latin skills through direct readings in Latin, using the textbook Lingua Latina Per Se Illustrata. Latin III students continue to make linguistic connections to English and other modern languages. In addition to studying the language itself, students also continue to learn about Roman history and culture. Themes: Themes explored in Latin III include marriage and childbirth, medicine, Roman government, dinner parties, and mythology.

Students in Latin IV begin to read authentic Latin texts from the Ancient Roman world, with a focus on Latin inscriptions and poetry. While reading these texts, students continue to develop and expand their Latin skills, make linguistic connections to English and other modern languages, and learn about Roman history and culture. Themes: Themes explored in Latin IV include Latin inscriptions from the Roman world, and the poetry of Catullus and Martial.

Design, draw, paint and study Art in 2 and 3 dimensions. Pencil, pen, ink, charcoal, watercolor, cray pas, acrylic paint, clay are the materials used to explore and solve visual design problems. While predominantly a “hands on” course, students will also be asked to respond to art through reading and writing. This is a gateway class for all classes in the art department.

courses.description: This class focuses on a hands-on approach to a variety of fine and practical arts skills. While drawing is used as a fundamental skill, things like sewing, printmaking, jewelry making and clay are all part of the crafts movement. While this class serves as a foundation gateway class it is geared more towards the practical arts than the fine arts. If you like working with your hands, this is a good class for you. Much like foundations in art, this is a gateway class for all classes in the art department.
courses.fulfills_text: (Please note this course satisfies the Art graduation requirement)

courses.description: Studio Art Drawing is an intermediate course focusing on drawing and design skills. Students will be exposed to a range of media and techniques to enhance their skills. A strong emphasis is also placed on composition. Students who have completed Foundations in Art or who have a waiver based on a submitted portfolio of drawing may qualify for the class. All abilities are welcome and evaluation is based on student improvement over the course of the semester vs. innate talent. This is predominantly a “hands on” class and also explores art history through presentations and web journeys. Portfolio development is supported.
courses.prerequisites: Foundations of Art (Traditional class)

courses.description: An intermediate course focused on developing an understanding of paint and color. Students will explore color through a variety of materials and techniques. While predominantly a “hands on” course, students will increase their understanding of color theory, art history, and composition, and be asked to respond to art through reading and writing. A partial list of materials may include pastel, watercolor, acrylic paint, and mixed media. *This course is offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT.
courses.prerequisites: Studio Art 1 (Drawing and Design)
courses.notes: Dual enrollment (college credit) course per catalog; see DUAL ENROLLMENT, pp.15-18

courses.description: Ceramics are used throughout the world in myriad cultures for both their function and their form. Through hands-on projects students will develop patience and discipline while working with clay. Ceramic projects take a long time to complete from wet clay through two firings to a finished piece. This course requires students to balance production of multiple projects with good studio practice. Clay is a messy medium and students are required to maintain studio cleanliness; they will be given chores to help do so. The first half of the course is structured around developing skills with different techniques used to manipulate clay (e.g. slab building, coiling, sculpting, coiling, etc). The second half of the course is structured around artistic problems or questions that require students to think about the design, function, and aesthetics that they will use to solve the problem(s) posed. There is a lab fee of $10.00, which students are expected to pay. This fee helps to partially cover material, firing, and maintenance costs. Finances are different for everyone and if you have concerns you may talk to the teacher or to counseling if you are more comfortable. We may decide to waive the fee.
courses.prerequisites: Strongly recommend Foundations (Traditional class)

courses.description: This course offers disciplined and motivated students the opportunity to continue to develop skills in different techniques working with clay through hands-on projects. Students will be presented with artistic questions which they will have to explore through the medium of clay. The second part of the course is designated for students to work independently to develop their own series of work with a written artist statement to accompany it. There is a lab fee of $10.00, which students are expected to pay. This fee helps to partially cover material, firing, and maintenance costs. Finances are different for everyone and if you have concerns you may talk to the teacher or to counseling if you are more comfortable. We may decide to waive the fee. *This course is offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT.
courses.prerequisites: Ceramics 1 with a grade of 75 or above or with department head approval.
courses.notes: Dual enrollment (college credit) course per catalog; see DUAL ENROLLMENT, pp.15-18

courses.description: This advanced course is tailored for self-motivated and disciplined students eager to elevate their proficiency in clay artistry through diverse techniques and hands-on projects. Emphasizing autonomy and creative exploration, students will grapple with profound artistic inquiries, using clay as a dynamic medium for expression. In the latter part of the course, students are empowered to chart their own artistic trajectory, developing a personalized series of work alongside a comprehensive written artist statement. This innovative approach encourages students to shape their unique vision within the realm of clay art. *This course is offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT.
courses.prerequisites: Ceramics 2 with a grade of 75 or above or with department head approval.
courses.notes: Dual enrollment (college credit) course per catalog; see DUAL ENROLLMENT, pp.15-18

courses.description: Sculpture an intermediate level art class, allows students who have completed Foundations in Art to continue to work on 3 dimensional design problems. The assignments and materials provide a greater challenge than Foundations in Art, and students are given more creative freedom within the assignment framework. In keeping with the departmental philosophy, Sculpture is a discipline based art program in which students learn design theory, art history relevant to their work, and are required to think critically about their work. Various sculptural processes such as casting, relief sculpture, subtractive and additive processes are undertaken and some materials include wood, plaster, clay, and wire. While predominantly a "hands on" course, students will be asked to respond to art through reading and writing. Students will be expected to pay a $10 lab fee at the beginning of the course.
courses.prerequisites: Strongly recommend Foundations of Art (traditional class) or Art of Crafts

courses.description: This course is designed to build on the 3-dimensional design skills learned in Sculpture I and to create at an advanced level. Students will utilize their prior knowledge of color and surface quality, the work of great sculptors past and present, and technical skills to work “in the round” and relief. Casting, multi- piece molds, additive and subtractive methods will be part of the Sculpture II curriculum. Students will have the opportunity to work in teams to create public art that enhances the community. In addition to the creation of sculpture, students are expected to articulate their knowledge and experience through writing and class discussions. *This course is offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT.
courses.prerequisites: Fine and Practical Art course and Sculpture I with a grade of 75 or above or with department head approval.
courses.notes: Dual enrollment (college credit) course per catalog; see DUAL ENROLLMENT, pp.15-18

courses.description: This course is a fusion of fiber art, fabrics and fashion. This course is geared towards beginning students’ exposure to technical knowledge in sewing and supports the artist sewer in problem solving creative projects. Sewing machine mechanics, accessories, and maintenance are explained and explored. Students will be introduced to many different types of fabrics, pattern making, hand sewing techniques, notions and more. Class time is mainly hands-on project time. This course draws upon the creative side of students to tap into artistic sewing pieces which may use non-traditional materials or non-traditional sewing craft. A wide variety of fabric is available in the classroom in addition to upcycled clothing donations in support of the art department's efforts of reducing environmental impact. This class includes an introductory fashion drawing unit which assists in satisfying the art graduation requirement or a student’s desire to take additional sewing or drawing coursework.
courses.fulfills_text: (Please note this course satisfies the Art graduation requirement)

courses.description: Independence and freedom in project choice will build on your previous learning. This course is for the student who is interested in learning more sewing and fiber art techniques in addition to having more freedom and project choice. As in Sewing 1, class time is largely hands-on with exploration in quilting, applique, knitting, crewel needlepoint and so much more. A wide variety of fabric is available in the classroom in addition to the upcycled clothing donations in support of the art departments’ efforts of reducing environmental impact. Students will learn how to apply their knowledge gained in Sewing 1 as well as complete a unit on fashion design.
courses.prerequisites: Sewing 1

courses.description: Students will learn about creating living environments that meet specific design concepts and needs. Through design projects students will create hands-on projects that relate to interior design alongside the textbook curriculum. Projects will revolve around drafting, furniture arrangement, and how to execute a storyboard for visual presentation. Storyboards will be created both by hand and by digital apps such as Canva. Art concepts covered are the elements of design, principles of design, and the role of color. This class is for the student who likes to take a personal style vision and develop it into a workable living space. Must have basic knowledge of measuring in order to successfully complete required floor plan drawings. This class is a good prerequisite for sewing and general art classes.
courses.fulfills_text: (Please note this course satisfies the Art graduation requirement)

courses.description: A studio course designed to build on the artistic skills acquired in the intermediate classes. Advanced techniques, materials, and concepts are explored through teacher presented studies and student developed projects. Student expression and independence is encouraged with teacher guidance. Portfolio development, both digitally and through collected work, can be used to facilitate entrance to art schools and related university studies. Techniques include drawing, printmaking, painting, 2D and 3D design, and non-traditional materials. Selected readings in art history and contemporary art will facilitate discussions and written responses. This course may be repeated for credit. *This course may also be offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT.
courses.prerequisites: Studio Art I and II
courses.notes: Catalog notes this course may also be offered for college credit (see DUAL ENROLLMENT)

courses.description: AP Art will be a full year class and will replace the Advanced Art in the Community class as the Capstone for Visual and Performing Arts students. It will also be open to other juniors and seniors who have taken an advanced level of art. The class will heavily focus on portfolio development and strategies to be a successful working artist. The AP class will focus on sustained investigation, experimentation and communication of ideas in 2D and 3D art. It will focus on the development of skills, processes and concepts.

courses.description: ● Students will learn the basic skills of graphic design (or digital art making) using industry standard, Mac based software. ● Students will produce digital and printed media using the following programs: Adobe Photoshop, Adobe Illustrator and Adobe InDesign. ● Students will learn to use the scanning equipment, digital camera file uploading, transferring and downloading files legally, making pdf files and other useful skills related to graphic arts.
courses.prerequisites: None (prior experience and knowledge in the arts recommended)
courses.fulfills_text: (Please note, this course satisfies the Art graduation requirement)

courses.description: ● Students will take the basic skills learned in Computer Graphic Design I and apply them to producing more advanced graphic design artwork. ● Students will develop lifelong skills and prepare for post-secondary studies through creative projects and portfolio development. ● Students will have the opportunity to work independently and explore other media such as Weebly, Wix and After Effects. ● Students will connect with the school and local community to produce digital artwork for community events and programs (ie. logos, posters, web design, banners, newsletters, etc.). ● Students taking this course need to possess the ability to work independently and in groups, to be self-motivated, to be able to take constructive artistic criticisms and to be fluent in the Adobe software programs learned in Graphic Design I. ● This course may also be offered for optional college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT.

courses.description: This course is designed for the interested photography student. Photo I covers all aspects of digital photography within an artistic context. Students will also be introduced to Digital Cameras, Adobe Lightroom, & Photoshop. 35mm photography is accessible for Photo I. Students will learn digital processing, how to print digitally processed photos. Students are expected to work independently, shooting photos after school, at home and during class (when specified). Course work includes shooting assignments, photo history, weekly journals, and a research paper/presentation on a personally selected photographer and the art of photography. Some cameras are available on loan for student use, but it is strongly recommended that you supply your own digital camera if possible.
courses.fulfills_text: Digital Art Requirement

courses.description: This course is designed for the motivated photography student. This is a continuation of the Photography 1 course. It covers all aspects of digital photography while introducing more advanced camera, lighting, and editing techniques. Students will have the opportunity to explore different photographic subjects and printing processes. Studio lighting will be introduced and used to gain a technical understanding of light and camera functions. Emphasis will be placed on independently developed challenges for each project, weekly journals, and monthly “revisits” of missed photographic opportunities. A cohesive portfolio of finished work will be expected of each student at the end of the term, including a digital portfolio. Some cameras are available on loan for student use, it is strongly recommended that the student supply their own digital camera if possible. *This course might also be offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT
courses.prerequisites: Photography 1 with a grade of 75 or above or with department head approval.
courses.notes: Catalog notes this course may also be offered for college credit (see DUAL ENROLLMENT)

courses.description: This course is designed for the passionate photography student. This student will be self-guided but will work in the structure of the Photography 2 class with much higher expectations in the quality of produced work and more advanced challenges will be given to Photo 3 students with each assignment. A weekly journal is required along with review of missed photographic opportunities. Emphasis will be placed on student developed independent work. An extensive portfolio of work is required for the culmination of the course. Some cameras are available on loan for student use, but it is strongly recommended that the student supply their own digital camera if possible. *This course might also be offered for college credit; see DUAL ENROLLMENT
courses.prerequisites: Photography II with a grade of 75 or above or with department head approval.
courses.notes: Catalog notes this course may also be offered for college credit (see DUAL ENROLLMENT)

courses.description: An independent project in art requires the student to have a strong sense of purpose and personal responsibility. This is not intended to duplicate existing courses. Content should be determined by the student in close consultation with the instructor prior to submitting the application to Mrs. Parker. The Art faculty is limited to no more than 3 independent students at any time, so Independent Studies will be competitive and limited.
courses.prerequisites: Approval of instructor and Department Head

courses.description: Food Fundamentals will teach you how to be comfortable in the kitchen through hands-on cooperative learning. You will learn about food preparation techniques, proper equipment usage, meal planning, purchasing techniques, nutrition, consumer issues, regional food and foreign food. You will explore the nutrient value in food, how appetite appeal affects what you eat, the social significance of how food plays into our choices, and cultural aspects of food. Students will have opportunities to have community guests in the classroom.
courses.notes: Sub-heading: Family Consumer Sciences (credits satisfy elective requirements)

courses.description: Using the skills learned in Foods Fundamentals students will further develop their skills with more advanced learning, community connections and hands-on food labs. This advanced study is based on nutrition, new food investigation, advanced cooking techniques, and the understanding of where food comes from along with recipe development. Curriculum is based on students interest and skill level.
courses.prerequisites: Food Fundamentals
courses.notes: Sub-heading: Family Consumer Sciences (credits satisfy elective requirements)

courses.description: This class is designed to teach students how professional recordings are made and will give them the knowledge and tools to begin recording themselves at a high level. We will dive into how to use a DAW (digital audio workstation) to record, mix and master music. We will also learn about the different types of microphones, microphone placement, and other recording techniques that lead to high quality recordings. In addition to recording sound in a DAW, we will use midi controllers to create our own music in the class. By the end of this class, students will have an understanding of how to create a high quality recording of singers and instrumentalists. From the initial recording, to production after the fact. They will also learn how to create their own music using a DAW.
courses.fulfills_text: A graduation credit in the arts can be earned in music classes.

courses.description: Students who take this class will learn the basics of rock band instruments such as drums, bass, guitar and keyboard. They will learn from the teacher, peer mentors, and by self-teaching. As students advance their playing skills, they will have the chance to collaborate with one another in listening to songs they like and figuring out how to play the songs themselves. In addition to playing instruments, the class will listen to music from different eras and discuss the history and meaning behind the songs. Students will also have the chance to dabble in using Soundtrap to produce music electronically. Students will have homework and projects as part of this class.

courses.description: Students will learn about and practice different skills that help them to write complete songs. This will include learning about song form/sections, melody, harmony, and rhythm. Students will study parts of language, learning how to use synonyms, adjectives, adverbs, imagery, and syllable count to write great lyrics. They will also work on their singing and learn how to play the guitar and learn what kinds of chord progressions support everyday songwriting. Students will work individually as well as in groups to sing, play, record, and give feedback to one another as they complete a variety of songwriting assignments.

courses.description: Chorus is a full-year, four-credit class. All chorus members are required to attend all concerts in which the ensemble is performing, including evening concerts in November, March and May. Chorus students are taught about healthy and functional vocal technique, learn music literacy skills, and experience a wide variety of musical styles. Students are placed into sections (soprano, alto, tenor, and bass) and learn to sing advanced harmonies in 4- and 8-parts. Emphasis is placed on diction, dynamics, breath support, register use, expression, and interpretation. The chorus sings songs in many genres, meters, tempos, languages, arrangements and moods. While students learn to sing in a group, they are asked to reflect on their own musical identity and growth through class discussions and assignments. Students enrolling should be prepared to make this year-long commitment to the ensemble they are joining. If a student needs to enroll in Chorus for a single semester for two credits due to a schedule conflict, permission must be granted by the teacher prior to the beginning of the school year. This single semester option does not apply to students in grade nine.
courses.prerequisites: Willingness and ability to participate fully by singing throughout all rehearsals and concerts. Previous chorus experience is highly recommended but not required.
courses.fulfills_text: A graduation credit in the arts can be earned in music classes.

courses.description: Piano and Voice Studio is designed for students who are already BUHS Chorus. This class will meet every other day, opposite of Chorus. We will be learning proper vocal technique and expanding our keyboard skills. We will practice singing and playing our own parts in ensemble music, prepare for auditions, and practice solo works. We will learn how to effectively pick a solo work for your voice level, and how to develop it with guidance of the teacher. While this class is not an ensemble class, you will need to be ready to sing/play every day.

It is designed to offer vocal repertoire and class assignments that challenge students who are already familiar with vocal/choral technique and can sing in a small group setting. Vocalists auditioning for this ensemble must already be enrolled in chorus. This group meets one night per week with required attendance at all rehearsals and performances throughout the school year. Students are expected to practice their parts on their own each week at home. They will be given practice assignments (vocal practice tracks will be provided), and will periodically need to turn in recordings of themselves singing their songs for grades and credit. Students perform at regularly scheduled school concerts as well as community events around Brattleboro.

courses.description: Band is a full year, four credit class. Band students in all grade levels rehearse and perform together in one band. This performance course is designed to foster an understanding and love of music and music making as well as developing instrumental skills, artistic expression, and creativity. In large and small ensemble settings, band students will explore various musical styles and genres with a focus on standard and contemporary concert band literature as well as arrangements of Broadway and film scores, pop, and rock music. Instrument lessons scheduled during the school day are required for all band members and enable instruction to be differentiated for various instruments and ability levels. Individual achievement is monitored and guided through the use of performance assessments, both in the form of recorded playing tests and live solo performances. A regular routine of home practice is required as is attendance at all group performances, most of which happen outside of the school day. Students enrolling should be prepared to make this full year commitment to the ensemble. If a student needs to enroll in band for a single semester for two credits, permission must be granted by the teacher prior to the beginning of the school year. Students enrolled for a single semester must demonstrate proficiency in all of the performance indicators to earn course credit.

The curriculum combines an applied study of repertoire with introductory jazz theory and improvisation. Enrollment is strictly by audition and is limited to the standard jazz big band instrumentation of 2 alto saxes, 2 tenor saxes, 1 baritone sax, 4-5 trumpets, 4 trombones, piano, guitar, bass, and drums. Wind players and drummers must also be enrolled in Band. Music reading skills are required for all members. Jazz improvisation is a component of the class, although not the focus of the class. The class meets one night a week for two hours. The ensemble performs at all band concerts with occasional additional performances. Attendance at all evening rehearsals and performances is mandatory. Jazz Band is a full year, two-credit class. Students enrolling in the class should be prepared to make this year-long commitment to the ensemble they are joining and students are expected to practice their individual music parts on their own each week at home.

courses.description: Fundamentals of Music is a course dedicated to teaching the basic concepts that all musicians should know. This class is designed for all students, whether or not you are already involved in the music department at BUHS. Students will learn skills and concepts such as how to read notes, read rhythm and navigate a piece of music. We will also spend time learning basic music theory such as how to read a key signature, time signature, and how to build a scale. Listening to music is also a large part of this class. We will learn active listening skills and use them as we listen to music from different time periods in our history. Additionally, we will spend time learning instruments, particularly piano.

courses.description: *Ability to read and play notes as written on a staff. This course is for vocal and instrumental students who are interested in playing jazz. Students will play jazz standards, learning how to interpret and enhance a melody, read chord symbols, drill scale and patterns, and ultimately improvise through a tune. We will also do a lot of listening to the recordings of jazz masters and contemporary musicians, discussing and emulating their singing and playing. We will learn some jazz history in order to understand the origins of this great music and pay our respects to it. Finally, we will learn how to prepare for a jam session or gig, as well as how to work with a band. The class will visit the Vermont Jazz Center to take advantage of their resources and events.
